items.question: We created src/domain, src/application, and src/infrastructure folders and moved our files into them. Do we now have a layered architecture?
items.answer: No. Layering is a claim about dependency direction: stable business rules must not import volatile UI or transport details. Folder names enforce nothing; a component can still import the HTTP client directly and domain code can still import React. The separation only pays off when the import direction is real, typically enforced with lint or dependency rules, and when it reduces coupling enough to make tests or migrations easier.
items.trap: The naive answer treats directory structure as the architecture. Renaming folders changes nothing about the import graph, so you get the ceremony of four layers with none of the decoupling. The rule is responsibility and dependency direction, not file extension or folder name.

items.question: Our app is small and a component calls fetch directly. Is that a violation we must fix immediately?
items.answer: Not necessarily. The boundary is pragmatic: a small app may not need four layers. The cost of the direct call is coupling UI to transport details, which shows up later as harder tests and migrations. Fix it when that coupling starts to hurt, and use the practical test: does the separation reduce coupling and make tests or migrations easier?
items.trap: Both extreme answers fail. 'Always forbidden' adds ceremony a two-person app cannot pay for, while 'fine forever' ignores that the coupling compounds silently. The bank keeps the boundary explicitly pragmatic rather than absolute.

items.question: Two features need the same button. Should it move to the shared area right away?
items.answer: Not automatically. Shared code couples otherwise unrelated features, so the default is to keep them separate until the button proves to be a stable primitive with a clear owner. Promote it when it reflects a genuine shared concern, and expose it through the shared area's public API. The boundary should reflect change and ownership, not a drive to eliminate duplication.
items.trap: The reflexive DRY answer ('never duplicate, share immediately') creates a module that unrelated features now evolve together, which is exactly the coupling feature organization exists to avoid. The bank warns against forcing every tiny function into a feature or into shared code.

items.question: How do you actually stop feature A from importing feature B's internals, since both sit in the same repository?
items.answer: Folder layout alone cannot stop it. You need explicit import rules, enforced mechanically (lint or dependency-rule tooling), plus a small public API per feature that other features may consume. The rule is: reach a feature only through its public entry, never into its internals.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes the directory structure itself is the boundary. Nothing about colocated folders prevents a deep import; without enforced rules the boundary erodes one 'temporary' import at a time, and the ownership and deletion benefits disappear.

items.question: The feature works perfectly in Vite's dev server. Does that prove the production build will behave the same?
items.answer: No. Vite's dev server is native-ESM-oriented development, while production is a separate bundling flow with configurable targets, entries, and code splitting (https://vite.dev/guide/build). The two pipelines are different, so a dev-server success only proves the dev pipeline. Validate representative flows against the built artifact before shipping.
items.trap: The common assumption is that the dev server is a live preview of the production bundle. Because development and production are different flows in Vite, 'works in dev' is not evidence about the bundled output, and teams that ship on dev-server confidence discover the differences late.

items.question: Vite benchmarks faster than webpack, so the choice is made. What is wrong with that reasoning?
items.answer: Choosing from benchmark slogans ignores the constraints that actually decide the tool: required framework plugins, SSR or library output, browser targets, Module Federation needs, ecosystem maturity, build and HMR feedback, and the team's ability to own the configuration. Measure a representative application in your own repo, compare correctness as well as speed, and pick the smallest toolchain that satisfies deployment, compatibility, extensibility, and operational requirements.
items.trap: The naive answer treats speed as the only requirement. A faster tool that cannot express your federation, SSR, or browser-target requirements is not a candidate at all; the bank explicitly says to choose from constraints, not benchmark slogans.

items.question: Why not make the entry point convenient and re-export everything from index.ts?
items.answer: Because a giant barrel is the opposite of a narrow contract. Turborepo's repository guidance notes that barrel files can be difficult for compilers and bundlers and recommends explicit exports instead (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/structuring-a-repository). A barrel also turns every internal name into de facto public API, so internal refactors ripple to every consumer. Keep exports narrow, document compatibility expectations, and test the public surface as an API.
items.trap: The convenience answer optimizes for shorter import paths today at the cost of compiler and bundler behavior and a public surface you can never shrink. Explicit exports are the documented recommendation; a barrel-by-default is the documented anti-pattern.

items.question: A consumer imports @acme/ui/dist/internal/button.js and it works today. Where is the problem?
items.answer: It works only because the internal path is currently reachable; it is not a contract. The package's package.json exports should enumerate the entry points other packages may use and avoid exposing implementation files (https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#exports), so internal refactors do not become repository-wide edits. Replace the deep import with the public entry and let the exports map block future escapes.
items.trap: 'It compiles, so it is fine' confuses current reachability with a supported contract. The moment the package reorganizes its output, the consumer breaks with no version bump or deprecation signal, which is precisely what public entry points exist to prevent.

items.question: What happens at install time if a dependency declared with workspace: is missing locally at the requested version?
items.answer: Installation fails. The workspace: protocol tells pnpm to resolve only to a matching local workspace package, so there is no silent fallback to the registry (https://pnpm.io/workspaces). That failure is the feature: accidental version drift or a missing package surfaces at install instead of shipping as a registry copy nobody intended.
items.trap: The common assumption is that pnpm will 'helpfully' fall back to the registry version. Silent fallback is exactly the failure mode the protocol exists to prevent; the loud install failure is the desired, deterministic behavior.

items.question: If we publish this package, do consumers need pnpm and workspace semantics?
items.answer: No. When the package is published, pnpm replaces the workspace specification with an ordinary version or semver range, so consumers install it like any other dependency. The protocol is a local-development contract, not a publishing format; the remaining work is managing versions and compatibility of the published public contract.
items.trap: The fear that workspace: leaks into the published manifest and breaks npm or yarn consumers is backwards: pnpm rewrites it on publish. Worrying about the protocol string distracts from the real job, which is release and compatibility management of the public API.

items.question: Your builds were missing cache too often, so you narrowed inputs to src/** and hit rates improved. What may you have just broken?
items.answer: Cache correctness. inputs define what contributes to the task's cache hash; once you omit files that affect the output (task configuration such as vite.config.ts, lockfiles, generated inputs, or environment values the task reads), two runs can share a hash while needing different outputs, so a hit restores stale artifacts. Turborepo's docs also warn that specifying inputs opts out of the default behavior of hashing all source-controlled files in the package (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks). Narrow only with evidence that omitted files cannot affect the result, and verify with a dry run or run summaries.
items.trap: The naive view treats a cache hit as proof of correctness. A hit only proves the hashed inputs match; anything left out of the hash is invisible to the cache, so 'faster' here can literally mean 'restoring the wrong build'.

items.question: You removed dependsOn: ['^build'] from the app's build task and CI got faster. Why is that dangerous?
items.answer: dependsOn is what makes a package's direct dependencies build first. Without ^build, the app's build can run against missing or stale dependency artifacts; Turborepo's own documentation shows this class of bug with type checking, where a package hits cache despite a dependency's interface having changed (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks). The speedup comes from deleting a correctness guarantee, not from doing the same work faster.
items.trap: The naive read is 'fewer dependencies means a leaner pipeline'. The ^ prefix encodes the package-graph edge; removing it lets a cache hit in the app survive a breaking change in the library it consumes, which is a stale-artifact bug, not an optimization.

items.question: App A depends on lib L in the project graph. When you run tests, must A's test wait for L's test?
items.answer: No, not automatically. The project graph records source and dependency relationships; the task graph records concrete targets and the task-to-task dependencies needed for one invocation. A's test only waits for L's test if a task relationship such as ^test is configured (https://nx.dev/concepts/mental-model). Architecture, scheduling, and cache invalidation are separate decisions.
items.trap: The common conflation is 'project dependency implies every target waits for the dependency's same-named target'. That turns the task graph into a mirror of the project graph and serializes work that has no actual ordering requirement.

items.question: When Nx computes affected projects, which graph is it using?
items.answer: The project graph. Nx uses the project graph to calculate affected projects, then creates the smallest relevant task graph for the invocation. The distinction matters: affected is a source-dependency question, while what actually runs, in what order, and what is cached is a task-graph question.
items.trap: The naive answer treats 'affected' as a task-graph concept and expects it to reason about targets. If affected were computed from the task graph, refactoring a build relationship would change which projects count as affected, which is not how source-level impact works.

items.question: The team sets VITE_DEBUG=false in production, but verbose logging still turns on. Why?
items.answer: Because env values are strings. import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG is the string 'false', which is truthy in JavaScript, so a truthiness check enables logging exactly when you meant to disable it. Parse booleans, numbers, and URLs at a typed configuration boundary instead of trusting raw strings (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode).
items.trap: The naive assumption is that Vite coerces 'false' to boolean false. It does not; every value arrives as a string. The same root cause breaks strict comparisons too, since 'true' === true is false, so both the truthiness and the === true versions of the naive check fail.

items.question: You added VITE_API_URL to .env.production, but CI keeps deploying with the old URL. The file is committed correctly. What should you check?
items.answer: Precedence and process. Vite documents that shell environment variables have higher priority than .env files, so a variable exported in the CI pipeline overrides .env.production. Also remember the dev server must be restarted after changing env files; values are read when the server or build starts, not continuously (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode).
items.trap: The naive answer assumes the file is the single source of truth. Because shell variables win, the .env file can be perfectly correct and still never be used; debugging env problems requires checking the whole precedence chain, not just the file.

items.question: Our application is huge. Does size alone justify micro-frontends?
items.answer: No. Micro-frontends are justified when independent delivery and team autonomy solve a real organizational or migration problem, not merely because the application is large (https://single-spa.js.org/docs/microfrontends-concept/). The browser is still one runtime, so DOM ownership, navigation, authentication, accessibility, observability, failure handling, and shared dependencies all need explicit rules, and those rules cost more than a modular single app until autonomy actually pays for itself.
items.trap: The naive scaling story treats boundaries as free. Each extra boundary adds runtime and operational cost inside a single runtime; if teams could already ship independently inside one deployable, the micro-frontend overhead buys nothing.

items.question: If we go micro-frontends, each team can pick its own framework. Isn't that the point?
items.answer: Framework freedom is a cost, not the goal. Prefer one framework where practical: multiple frameworks can be useful during a migration but increase runtime and operational cost. The point is independent delivery with the least coupling that achieves it, plus a path to consolidate when autonomy no longer pays for itself.
items.trap: The naive answer equates autonomy with technological maximalism. Multi-framework runtimes multiply the integration contract (shared dependencies, accessibility, observability, failure handling) for no delivery benefit when teams could have been autonomous within one framework.

items.question: Why does the host break when it treats a remote module like a normal static import?
items.answer: Because a remote module is asynchronous. Loading the remote container and evaluating the exposed module are separate steps: the host initializes a share scope, passes it to the container's init, and only then obtains the module through get (https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/). A static, synchronous import assumes all of that has already happened, which is not guaranteed at module-evaluation time.
items.trap: The naive mental model is 'an import with a different URL'. Federation remotes are runtime, asynchronous containers; treating them as local modules ignores the init and get handshake and the async boundary the host must establish first.

items.question: Host and remote both list React in shared, so it should be deduped. Why do hooks still throw about multiple React copies?
items.answer: Sharing is negotiated, not automatic. Shared dependencies are registered in a share scope, and version requirements plus singleton settings decide which copy is consumed. If the host and remote declare incompatible version ranges, or singleton is not set for a stateful library like React, the runtime can load two copies and hook state breaks. React-like libraries need an intentional compatibility policy, not just a shared entry.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes shared: { react } means 'one React, guaranteed'. The share scope picks among available versions based on requirements; without compatible ranges and a singleton policy for stateful libraries, deduplication silently fails at runtime.

items.question: Our application source code will not change in the migration, so behavior cannot change either. Right?
items.answer: Wrong. A build tool is part of the platform contract: changing it can alter module resolution, transforms, chunking, and debugging even when application source code stays unchanged. That is why the evaluation compares correctness as well as speed on a representative branch, validates deployment artifacts and developer workflows, and documents unsupported cases instead of trusting 'same code, same result'.
items.trap: The naive view treats the bundler as a transparent pipe. In reality it decides how modules resolve and how output is chunked, so identical source can produce different runtime behavior, different bundles, and a different debugging experience under a different tool.

items.question: How do you actually decide, then, if not by the speedup number?
items.answer: Define the workload and success metrics first: cold start, incremental rebuild, production build, output size, source maps, test and preview parity, memory, and CI cost. Inventory existing loader and plugin behavior, framework integration, custom transforms, aliases, asset handling, SSR, and federation requirements. Then run a representative branch with observability, compare correctness as well as speed, and use a reversible migration boundary.
items.trap: The naive single-metric evaluation on build time hides the ways a bundler change regresses: broken transforms, different chunking, worse source maps, or CI cost shifts that a benchmark never measures.

items.question: The team finished moving all files into the new structure last sprint. Isn't the migration done?
items.answer: No. A migration is complete when the old constraint is removed, not when a new folder exists beside it. If the old path, adapters, or dual build still exist, you are paying for both architectures and the old constraint still governs. Delete the old path only after ownership, monitoring, rollback, and adoption are proven.
items.trap: The naive answer equates 'files moved' with 'migration complete'. Until the legacy path is deleted, the codebase carries two architectures and every future change must still respect the old constraint, which is the opposite of the migration's goal.

items.question: Wouldn't it be faster to freeze the app for a quarter and rewrite it in one go?
items.answer: It feels faster and is usually riskier. Freezing stops delivery, removes the feedback loop, and makes the cutover a single unrecoverable bet. The incremental path keeps release capability: compatibility adapters at a narrow seam, one route or feature at a time, both paths testable, small commits, and contract tests around APIs, analytics, routing, and shared UI, so progress is observable and rollback is always available.
items.trap: The naive answer compares calendar durations, not risk. A big-bang cutover has no rollback, no intermediate verification, and no learning; the incremental approach trades a longer calendar for the ability to ship, measure, and reverse at every step.

items.question: Ops wants one Docker image promoted through dev, staging, and prod. We'll just keep using .env.production and .env.staging. What is wrong?
items.answer: Mode-specific env files are selected at build time, so each mode produces a different artifact; that contradicts the requirement of promoting one artifact. For a single artifact, separate build-time public values (typed and validated during the build, immutable once bundled) from non-secret runtime configuration injected at deployment or request time from a controlled server response, HTML bootstrap, or equivalent mechanism, and validate its schema before bootstrapping the app (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode).
items.trap: The naive answer mistakes Vite's env-and-mode system for runtime configuration. import.meta.env is build-time substitution; per-mode files mean per-mode builds, so 'one image, many environments' silently becomes 'many images'.

items.question: Fine, we'll inject the API secret at runtime instead of build time. Now it's safe, right?
items.answer: No. Changing when a value arrives does not change who can read it. A browser can inspect every value it receives, whether it was bundled at build time or fetched at runtime, so secrets must stay server-side on a backend or serverless function. Runtime injection is for non-secret configuration, with schema validation before bootstrap and explicit precedence and failure behavior.
items.trap: The naive answer treats the leak as a timing problem. The client bundle and any runtime response are both readable by the browser; 'injected later' only moves where the secret is visible, not whether it is visible.

items.question: Let's prevent duplication by putting all shared code in one big @acme/utils package. Good governance?
items.answer: No. The goal is fast, independent change with discoverable contracts, not maximum code sharing. A single giant shared utilities package couples unrelated teams, accumulates unowned dependencies, and pushes everyone toward synchronized releases. Code should become a package under an explicit policy, with narrow public APIs and dependencies declared locally per package.
items.trap: The naive answer optimizes for zero duplication and gets a distributed monolith: every change to utils is effectively a change to every consumer, which is precisely the coupling governance exists to prevent.

items.question: We're all in one repo with pnpm workspaces, so we can't end up as a distributed monolith. Right?
items.answer: Wrong. A monorepo is a repository strategy, not an architecture. Without explicit package ownership, narrow public APIs, dependency direction rules, and enforcement (tagging or lint rules, no filesystem escapes across package boundaries), a single repo can hide the same hidden coupling as many repos, plus the illusion of shared context. Measure affected CI time, cache hit rate, dependency fan-out, and change failure rate to keep the goal honest.
items.trap: The naive answer confuses repository layout with architectural decoupling. Coupling lives in imports and contracts, not in repo boundaries; a monorepo without governance is a distributed monolith with a single git history.

items.question: You're about to ship the second federated remote. What organizational policy must exist before it deploys?
items.answer: Treat the remote as a runtime dependency, not a local import with a URL. Before shipping: pin or select remote versions deliberately with versioned URLs, define behavior when a manifest or entry cannot load and when an exposed contract is missing, keep a known-good fallback where the product requires continuity, make loading, initialization, and rendering failures observable by remote and version, and assign ownership for shared libraries plus compatibility tests for exposed APIs. Webpack's documented mechanics (asynchronous remotes, share-scope version selection, duplicate output.uniqueName collisions, https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/) should be encoded as release, rollback, security review, and incident-response policy.
items.trap: The naive plan is 'each team ships its own remoteEntry and we'll handle problems when they happen'. Without version pinning, fallback, and observability by remote and version, a remote's breaking deploy becomes an unattributable outage of the whole shell.

items.question: A remote deployed a breaking change to an exposed component at 14:00. The host had zero deploys that day. Whose incident is it, and what would have caught it?
items.answer: It is a shared incident by design: the remote is a runtime dependency of the host, so the host's behavior changed without a host deploy. What would have caught it: compatibility tests for the exposed API run in the remote's pipeline against the host's contract, deliberate version pinning or selection so the breaking change did not reach the host automatically, and observability that attributes failures by remote and version so rollback is fast.
items.trap: The naive ownership model ('no host deploy, so not a host incident') assumes deployment boundaries equal dependency boundaries. Federation moves code across deployment boundaries at runtime, so contract testing and version policy, not deploy logs, define who breaks whom.

items.question: CI shows a full cache hit, but the deployed bundle contains last week's feature flag value. Name the likely cause classes.
items.answer: The fingerprint omitted an input that changes the output. The usual classes: environment variables used by the task but not declared in the cache model, task configuration or tool versions, lockfile changes, and generated inputs. Turborepo hashes inputs to decide whether to restore results and explicitly assumes tasks are deterministic (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/caching); Nx likewise hashes source, configuration, dependencies, and other inputs (https://nx.dev/concepts/mental-model). A hit only proves the hashed inputs match, so inspect the task definition, compare against a clean build, and use dry-run or summary output to find what differs.
items.trap: The naive reaction is 'the cache is broken'. The cache did exactly what it was told: the hash matched because a real input was never part of the hash. Debugging must focus on the cache model's declared inputs, not on cache machinery.

items.question: Our build writes a build timestamp into the bundle footer. Cache says hit, artifacts differ. What's the root cause?
items.answer: The task is nondeterministic: identical inputs produce different outputs because of the clock. Both Turborepo and Nx caching assume determinism, so caching this task is unsound: a hit can restore an artifact that does not correspond to a fresh run of the same inputs. Either make the task deterministic (move the timestamp to deployment time) or disable caching for that task.
items.trap: The naive answer hunts for a missing input to add to the hash. No input list can capture 'the current clock'; nondeterminism is a property of the task, not of the fingerprint, so the fix is removing the nondeterminism or opting the task out of caching.

items.question: The library worked inside the app, where it read process.env.NODE_ENV for dev logging. After a Vite library build, consumers see the wrong branch. Why?
items.answer: Because environment handling does not transfer from app builds to library builds. Vite documents that import.meta.env is statically replaced in library builds, while process.env is not automatically replaced (https://vite.dev/guide/build#library-mode). In the app, the app's build pipeline handled the substitution; in the library, the value depends on whatever the consumer's runtime does with process.env, if it defines it at all. Libraries should not import application-only environment assumptions.
items.trap: The naive assumption is that env handling is a property of the code. It is a property of the build: the same line behaves differently under an app build and a library build because only import.meta.env is statically replaced in library mode.

items.question: Why externalize React in a library build instead of bundling it in?
items.answer: A library must avoid forcing consumers to download or instantiate dependencies that should remain external. Vite's library mode recommends externalizing dependencies such as React, and the package then exposes the generated files through package.json (https://vite.dev/guide/build#library-mode). Bundling React in would duplicate it for every consumer and, for a stateful library, risk multiple React instances in one page.
items.trap: The naive answer optimizes for 'the library works standalone' and bundles everything. That duplicates dependencies across every consumer and can create the duplicate-instance bugs stateful libraries are prone to; externalization is the documented library-mode recommendation.

mcqs.question: In a layered frontend architecture, what actually makes the separation meaningful?
options: The dependency direction: stable business rules must not import volatile UI or transport details.
The folder names: code must live in folders named presentation, application, domain, and infrastructure.
The layer count: every serious app needs exactly four layers, and a small app is just an unfinished one.
The technology mix: each layer must use a different framework or library to prove independence.
mcqs.explanation: The rule is separation by responsibility, not by file extension: the names matter less than dependency direction, and a small app may not need four layers while a large app benefits when the separation reduces coupling and eases tests and migrations. The strongest distractor (folder names) fails because renaming folders changes nothing about the import graph: a component can still import an HTTP client directly, so the structure is cosmetic without an enforced dependency rule.

mcqs.question: A team organizes the frontend by features. Which practice actually preserves the benefit of that organization?
options: A global components/, hooks/, and utils/ tree kept alongside the features, so shared code has one home.
A small public API per feature plus enforced import rules, so no feature reaches into another feature's internals.
Free cross-folder imports between features, since everything lives in the same repository anyway.
Forcing every helper, however tiny, into a feature folder so that nothing is ever shared.
mcqs.explanation: Feature organization works when each feature exposes a small public API and import rules prevent reaching into another feature's internals, with genuinely shared code in an explicit shared area. The strongest distractor (the global tree) fails because it recreates the exact coupling feature organization exists to avoid: unrelated code becomes coupled in components, hooks, and utils folders, and ownership and deletion get harder. The last distractor overcorrects: stable primitives and cross-cutting infrastructure can remain shared.

mcqs.question: A user flow works in Vite's dev server. What does that prove about production?
options: It proves production works, because the dev server and the production build run the same module pipeline.
Nothing by itself: development is native-ESM-oriented serving while production is a separate bundling flow, so the built artifact must be validated on representative flows.
It proves production works as long as the dev server was started in production mode.
It proves nothing, because Vite has no production build and webpack must be added for deployment.
mcqs.explanation: Vite provides a dev server and a distinct production build flow with configurable targets, entries, and code splitting (https://vite.dev/guide/build), so a dev-server success only exercises the dev pipeline. The strongest distractor (same pipeline) fails because development and production are different flows in Vite; the last distractor fails in the opposite direction, since Vite does ship a production build, and the mode distractor fails because mode selection changes which env files load, not which pipeline serves the code.

mcqs.question: Why should a workspace package expose deliberate entry points through package.json exports?
options: So every internal file becomes importable from outside, giving consumers maximum flexibility.
Because a barrel file that re-exports everything is the recommended default entry point.
So consumers depend on supported names and contracts rather than the directory layout, letting internal refactors stay internal.
Because exports only matter for packages published to a registry, not for internal workspace packages.
mcqs.explanation: A public entry point is a boundary you can evolve deliberately: consumers depend on supported names and contracts, and the exports field can enumerate entry points while avoiding exposing implementation files (https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#exports). The strongest distractor (the barrel default) fails because Turborepo's guidance notes barrel files can be difficult for compilers and bundlers and recommends explicit exports (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/structuring-a-repository). The last distractor fails because boundaries matter inside the workspace too: deep imports turn internal refactors into repository-wide edits.

mcqs.question: A pnpm workspace package declares @acme/ui as workspace:*, but no local package matches at install time. What happens?
options: pnpm silently installs the best-matching @acme/ui from the registry so the build keeps moving.
pnpm creates a placeholder stub and prints a warning to address later.
pnpm rewrites the dependency to a plain semver range and retries the registry automatically.
Installation fails, because workspace: resolves only to a matching local workspace package.
mcqs.explanation: The workspace: protocol tells pnpm to resolve only to a matching local workspace package; if the requested local version is absent, installation fails, which exposes accidental version drift early and keeps local development and CI deterministic (https://pnpm.io/workspaces). The strongest distractor (silent registry fallback) describes exactly the failure mode the protocol was designed to prevent, and it is what would happen with a plain version spec.

mcqs.question: A Turborepo build task sets inputs to ["src/**"], but the build also reads vite.config.ts and the DEPLOY_ENV variable. What is the risk?
options: Cache hits can restore stale artifacts, because output-affecting inputs are missing from the hash.
No risk: Turborepo automatically discovers every config file and environment variable a task reads.
The task fails immediately with a missing-cache-input error, so the mistake is self-detecting.
Only the dev server is affected; production builds bypass the task cache entirely.
mcqs.explanation: A cache is only safe when all output-affecting inputs, including relevant environment values and configuration, are represented in the hash; Turborepo hashes inputs to decide whether to restore results and assumes tasks are deterministic (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/caching). Specifying inputs also opts out of the default behavior of hashing all source-controlled files in the package (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks). The strongest distractor (auto-discovery) fails because Turborepo hashes exactly what is declared: an undeclared env var is invisible to the fingerprint and nothing errors.

mcqs.question: In Nx, app A depends on lib L (a project-graph edge). What does that imply when running tests?
options: A's test automatically waits for L's test, because every project edge implies the same-named target dependency.
L's test waits for A's test, since dependents are validated before their dependencies.
Nothing automatic: A's test does not wait for L's test unless a task dependency such as ^test is configured.
Nx refuses to run both tests in one invocation and requires two separate commands.
mcqs.explanation: The project graph describes projects and their source or dependency relationships, while the task graph describes concrete targets and the task-to-task dependencies needed for one invocation; two projects can depend on a library while their test tasks run independently unless a ^test relationship is configured (https://nx.dev/concepts/mental-model). The strongest distractor fails because it mirrors the project graph onto the task graph, serializing work that has no ordering requirement and conflating architecture with scheduling.

mcqs.question: A Vite app gates verbose logging with: if (import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG). The env file sets VITE_DEBUG=false in production. What happens?
options: Verbose logging turns on: the value is the string "false", which is truthy.
The gate works, because Vite coerces "false" to boolean false at build time.
The build fails with a type error for using a string where a boolean is expected.
The variable is undefined in production, because VITE_ variables are only defined in development.
mcqs.explanation: Vite exposes VITE_-prefixed variables through import.meta.env as strings, so they must be parsed into booleans, numbers, and URLs at a typed configuration boundary (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode). The strongest distractor (automatic coercion) fails because no coercion happens; the same root cause breaks strict comparisons too, since 'true' === true is false. The last distractor misreads modes: files like .env.production exist precisely to define values for production builds.

mcqs.question: When is a micro-frontend architecture justified?
options: Whenever the codebase passes a size threshold, because large apps cannot be built any other way.
Whenever more than one team touches the frontend, since multiple teams require separate deployables.
Whenever teams want different frameworks, because framework freedom is the primary benefit.
When independent delivery and team autonomy solve a real organizational or migration problem, not merely because the application is large.
mcqs.explanation: Micro-frontends pay off when independent delivery and team autonomy solve a real organizational or migration problem; the browser is still one runtime where DOM ownership, navigation, authentication, observability, failure handling, and shared dependencies need explicit rules (https://single-spa.js.org/docs/microfrontends-concept/). The strongest distractor (team count) fails because multiple teams can ship independently inside one deployable; the framework-freedom distractor fails because multiple frameworks mainly make sense during migration and increase runtime and operational cost.

mcqs.question: Host and remote both declare React in Module Federation's shared config. Why might the page still end up with two React copies?
options: Share scopes choose a copy based on version requirements and singleton settings; incompatible ranges or a missing singleton policy can load multiple copies.
Federation always dedupes shared dependencies automatically, so two copies are impossible.
React cannot be listed in shared at all; each build must bundle it privately.
Duplicate output.uniqueName values always duplicate every shared dependency.
mcqs.explanation: Shared dependencies are registered in a share scope rather than necessarily bundled privately, and version requirements and singleton settings influence which shared copy is consumed, so stateful libraries like React need an intentional compatibility policy (https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/). The strongest distractor (automatic dedupe) fails because sharing is negotiated at runtime, not guaranteed. The uniqueName distractor confuses two documented failure modes: duplicate output.uniqueName values collide on the runtime name, they do not control share-scope version selection.

mcqs.question: One frontend artifact must be promoted unchanged through dev, staging, and production with different API URLs. What is the sound design?
options: Build a separate artifact per environment using .env.staging and .env.production, which keeps each build simple.
Keep everything in import.meta.env and treat it as a runtime configuration service the app reads after deploy.
Typed, validated build-time public values plus environment-specific non-secret values injected at deployment or request time and schema-validated before bootstrap.
Encrypt the secrets into the bundle and decrypt them in the browser at runtime, so only the app can read them.
mcqs.explanation: Build-time values are immutable once bundled, so a single promoted artifact needs non-secret runtime configuration injected from a controlled server response, HTML bootstrap, or equivalent deployment mechanism, with its schema validated before bootstrapping (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode). The strongest distractor (per-environment builds) fails because mode-specific env files are selected at build time, producing different artifacts, which is exactly what promotion forbids. The encryption distractor fails because a browser can inspect every value it receives; encryption the client can undo is not secrecy.

scenarios.prompt: This Vite app cannot turn debug logging off in production, and a security review flagged the config module. Find every defect and rewrite the configuration boundary.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Walkthrough: (1) The debug gate is broken because env values are strings: import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG is the string 'false', which is truthy, so verbose logging is enabled in production. The same root cause would break a === true check, since 'true' === true is false. (2) The payments secret is a leak: Vite bundles VITE_-prefixed variables into client code at build time, so anything prefixed VITE_ is public configuration and must never contain secrets. The charge call must go through a backend or serverless function that holds the secret server-side; the client only sends the card token to our own endpoint. (3) apiUrl is an unparsed string: parse it with new URL(...) at the boundary so a malformed value fails at startup or build time, not at the first fetch. (4) Nothing is validated: required public values should be validated at startup or build time so a missing VITE_API_URL fails loudly instead of producing undefined URLs. Rewrite: a single config module that reads import.meta.env once, parses and validates, and exports a typed object; the rest of the app imports typed config, never import.meta.env. Sketch: const raw = { apiUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, debug: import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG }; if (!raw.apiUrl) throw new Error('VITE_API_URL is required'); export const config = { apiUrl: new URL(raw.apiUrl), debug: raw.debug === 'true' };. Operationally, remember that shell variables have higher priority than .env files and that the dev server must be restarted after changing env files.
rubric: Identifies the string-truthiness bug: 'false' is a truthy string, so debug logging is on in production, and no automatic coercion exists.
Identifies the secret leak: VITE_ values are bundled into the client at build time, so the payments secret must move to a backend or serverless function.
Parses and validates at one typed boundary: URL construction, boolean parsing, and required-value checks instead of scattering raw strings.
States the operational facts: values are strings, shell variables override .env files, and the dev server needs a restart after env changes.
Keeps the fix at a single seam so application code imports a typed config module rather than import.meta.env directly.

scenarios.prompt: CI builds this monorepo. A pull request that only touched apps/web/src/** got a cache hit for the apps/web build task, and the staging deployment shipped production API URLs. The apps/web build script is `vite build`; its vite.config.ts reads process.env.DEPLOY_ENV to bake the API base URL into the bundle, and CI sets DEPLOY_ENV=staging on the staging pipeline. Diagnose the caching failure and fix the task definition.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Diagnosis: the cache is not broken, the cache model is. inputs defines what contributes to the task's hash, and the build's output depends on two things the hash never sees: apps/web/vite.config.ts (task configuration) and the DEPLOY_ENV environment variable. The PR changed only src files, so its hash matched the previously cached production build and Turborepo restored that artifact: a correct hit against an incomplete fingerprint. Note also that specifying inputs opts out of Turborepo's default behavior of hashing all source-controlled files in the package, so this narrowing is what removed vite.config.ts from the hash in the first place (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks). Fix: include the config file in inputs, for example ["src/**", "vite.config.ts"], or restore default behavior with ["$TURBO_DEFAULT$", "!README.md"]-style exclusions of files proven irrelevant; and declare DEPLOY_ENV as an environment cache input (the task-level env key, or globalEnv / globalDependencies when the value affects many tasks) so a changed value misses cache (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/caching). Keep outputs: ["dist/**"] so hits still restore the bundle. Verification: use --dry or --summarize to inspect what is actually hashed, and compare against a clean build when debugging a suspected stale hit. The governing principle: Turborepo assumes tasks are deterministic and hashes inputs to decide whether to restore results, so a cache hit is never evidence of correctness; narrow inputs only with proof that omitted files cannot affect the output.
rubric: Explains that a cache hit only proves the hashed inputs matched, and that the omitted config file and env var made the fingerprint incomplete rather than the cache broken.
Knows that specifying inputs replaces the default all-source-controlled-files behavior, which is how vite.config.ts fell out of the hash.
Fixes the task definition: config files added to inputs, DEPLOY_ENV declared as an environment cache input (env, or globalEnv/globalDependencies where appropriate), outputs kept.
Recommends verification tooling: dry runs or run summaries, and comparing against a clean build before trusting narrowed inputs.
Applies the determinism assumption and rejects 'cache hit equals correctness' reasoning when explaining the incident.

scenarios.prompt: Refactor this workspace UI package so consumers can only use a deliberate public API. Explain what breaks, why it breaks, and why the change is worth it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Problems: (1) The barrel re-exports everything, including the internal merge-styles helper, so every internal name is de facto public API; Turborepo's repository guidance notes that barrel files can be difficult for compilers and bundlers and recommends explicit exports (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/structuring-a-repository). (2) apps/marketing deep-imports @acme/ui/dist/internal/button, which works only because the path is currently reachable; it is not a contract, and a reorganization of the package's output would break it with no version bump or deprecation signal. (3) package.json uses main with no exports field, so nothing enumerates what consumers may use. Refactor: add an exports map that enumerates deliberate entry points, for example { ".": "./dist/index.js" } plus granular entries like "./button" only if consumers genuinely need them; keep the barrel small and explicit, exporting only public names and nothing from internal/; remove merge-styles from the public surface (inline it, or split it into its own package if it is genuinely shared); migrate the deep import in apps/marketing to the public entry as part of the same change; and test the public surface as an API so accidental exports fail CI. Payoff: internal refactors stop being repository-wide edits, ownership and API review become clear, dependency analysis works, and compilers and bundlers avoid barrel overhead. The package contract matters more than the source folder layout.
rubric: Adds a package.json exports map that enumerates entry points and stops exposing implementation files.
Removes internal exports from the barrel and keeps the public surface narrow, citing the compiler and bundler cost of giant barrels.
Migrates the existing deep import to the public entry instead of leaving a silently broken consumer.
Treats the public surface as a tested contract with documented compatibility expectations.
Justifies the change in terms of refactoring safety, ownership, and dependency analysis, not just tidiness.

scenarios.prompt: This shell mounts two federated remotes. Each remote works alone in its own dev server, but mounted together one remote's React hooks throw and the console shows a shared-scope version warning. Diagnose every defect against Module Federation's documented mechanics, then list the organizational policies that are missing.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Defects: (1) The shell statically imports both remotes at the top of its entry. A remote module is asynchronous: loading the container and evaluating the exposed module are separate steps, and the host must initialize a share scope, pass it to the container's init, and obtain modules through get (https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/). A synchronous import assumes that handshake has already happened, which is not guaranteed at module-evaluation time; the shell needs an async boundary before rendering remote content. (2) remote_two's config was copy-pasted and still declares name: 'remote_one'. Every build needs a unique runtime name to avoid collisions; duplicate output.uniqueName values are a documented failure mode, and two containers claiming the same runtime name can collide when mounted together. (3) The shared React policy is inconsistent: remote_one requires ^18.2.0 with singleton, remote_two requires ^18.0.0 without singleton. Share scopes choose which copy is consumed based on version requirements and singleton settings, so without a shared, intentional compatibility policy for a stateful library like React, the runtime can load two React copies and hook state breaks, which matches the hook errors and the shared-scope warning. Policies to define before more remotes ship: treat remotes as runtime dependencies of the shell, not imports with URLs; pin or select remote versions deliberately with versioned remote URLs; define behavior when a manifest or entry cannot load and when an exposed contract is missing; keep a known-good fallback where the product requires continuity; make loading, initialization, and rendering failures observable by remote and version; assign ownership for shared libraries; and run compatibility tests for exposed APIs in each remote's pipeline, with release, rollback, security review, and incident-response processes built on those mechanics.
rubric: Identifies the async violation: remotes load through container init and get, so a static import at entry evaluation is wrong and the shell needs an async boundary.
Identifies the duplicate name/uniqueName collision from the copy-pasted config as a documented failure mode.
Explains share-scope version selection and why consistent requiredVersion plus singleton matters for stateful libraries like React.
Proposes organizational policy: versioned remote URLs with deliberate pinning, fallback behavior, and failure observability by remote and version.
Frames remotes as runtime dependencies of the shell, including compatibility tests for exposed APIs and shared-library ownership.
